title: The Little Platoon: Edmund Burke on Loneliness and Belonging
excerpt: Edmund Burke argued that every larger loyalty grows from attachment to small, local groups he called little platoons. In this imagined letter he answers a reader who works from home in a new city and feels connected to everyone online but known by no one nearby.

sections.text:
You write to tell me that you moved to a new city for your work two years ago, that you do that work from a desk in your own rooms, and that you can go a whole week without speaking to anyone who knows your name. You have hundreds of acquaintances on your screens and no one you would ask to carry a sofa up the stairs. You ask whether something has gone wrong with the world or only with you.

I think a little of both, and I think the remedy is older and plainer than you expect.

sections.heading: Where Affection Begins
sections.text:
I was born in Dublin, the son of a Protestant attorney and a Catholic mother, and I spent part of my boyhood with my mother's people in the green country of County Cork. Later I was sent to a school at Ballitore kept by a Quaker, Abraham Shackleton, and his son Richard became my friend for the rest of my life. When I crossed to London as a young man, meant for the law and soon running from it, I carried those places with me. Whatever I later thought about nations and constitutions, I learned first in a kitchen, a schoolroom and a few muddy lanes.

That is the order in which love grows. In my book on the revolution in France I argued that a person's attachment to the small group they belong to, the family, the parish, the trade, the street, is the seed from which every larger loyalty grows. I called these groups little platoons. We do not love our country in the abstract and then come to love our neighbours as a special case of it. We love a few people and a few places, and then, if we are fortunate, the circle widens.

The men in Paris wanted it the other way round. They wanted to love humanity first, and they found that a person who loves only humanity is free to despise every human being in front of him. I fear your screens make a similar offer. They let you belong to vast crowds of the like-minded while the people on your own landing remain strangers. The crowd feels like company, but it cannot bring you soup when you are ill.

sections.heading: The Wisdom You Did Not Invent
sections.text:
You may tell me that the old forms of belonging are gone or were never much good. The church on your street is half empty, the lodge has closed, and the neighbours keep odd hours. I understand the temptation to conclude that you must design a new kind of community from nothing, fitted exactly to your own tastes.

Be slow to do that. I spent many pages defending what I called prejudice, by which I did not mean bigotry. I meant the judgment stored in habits and customs that no one living designed, because it was worked out by many generations through trial, failure and repair. A custom of calling on a new neighbour, of sitting down to the same supper every week, of turning up when someone in the parish has died, contains more knowledge about how people come to trust each other than any clever scheme you could draw up alone at your desk. You need not understand why a practice works before you take part in it. You only need to give it time.

So I would not tell you to invent your belonging. I would tell you to borrow it. Find an institution that was there before you arrived and will be there after you leave, a congregation, a choir, a volunteer fire company, a club that has met in the same room for fifty years, and join it on its own terms. You will find it slightly dull and slightly old-fashioned. That is usually a sign it has survived.

sections.heading: Manners Before Laws
sections.text:
Near the end of my life I wrote that manners matter more than laws, because laws touch us only now and then, while manners shape us every hour without our noticing, the way the air does. I meant it of whole nations, but it is just as true of a single life.

Loneliness is rarely cured by one great gesture. It yields to small courtesies repeated until they become habits. Learn the names of the people who serve you coffee. Knock on the door of the old woman downstairs when the weather turns. Go to the same places at the same hours so that your face becomes familiar. These things will feel trivial and even false at first, as if you were acting a part. Act it anyway. In my youth I wrote a small book about the beautiful and the sublime, and I observed there that sympathy and imitation are among the passions that bind people together, and that we learn our manners and opinions chiefly by imitating those around us, long before we reason about them. Habit does its work on the heart whether or not the heart has agreed in advance.

I found my own little platoons this way. In London I had no fortune and no family near me, and I made a home among friends. Some of us formed a club with Samuel Johnson and Joshua Reynolds and met to dine and argue for years. I married Jane Nugent, the daughter of the physician who had taken me into his house when I was unwell. Later I bought a farm at Beaconsfield and took a real interest in the crops and the people who worked them. None of it was grand. All of it held me up.

sections.heading: A Partnership Across Time
sections.text:
There is one more thing I would ask you to consider. I argued that society is a partnership not only among the living but among the living, the dead and those who are yet to be born. You are not only lonely in space. I suspect you are lonely in time as well, cut off from the people who made the street you live on and indifferent to the people who will inherit it.

Try to repair that too. Learn who built your neighbourhood and why. Tend something that will outlast you, a garden plot, a library, a charity, a child who is not your own. When I lost my surviving son, Richard, I compared myself to an old oak thrown down by a hurricane, with nothing left standing round me. What steadied me in my last years was work for others, among them a school I helped to found at Penn for the sons of French families who had fled the revolution. A person who is useful to the future is rarely alone, even on a quiet night.

You asked whether the fault lies with the world or with you. Your age has made it easy to live without obligations, and a life without obligations is a life without the ties that make us feel held. That is the world's part. Your part is to take on a few obligations freely, close to home, and keep them faithfully. Begin with one platoon. The rest will follow, slowly, as it always has.
